node.label: Jackson Lears
node.date_label: No Place of Grace (1981) · Fables of Abundance (1994) · Something for Nothing: Luck in America (2003)
node.description: A cultural historian of the United States whose work connects religious longing, commercial persuasion and the making of meaning. In his written exchange with B. R. Cohen he explains cultural history as an inquiry into meanings formed through lived anxieties and desires, including unintended consequences. Advertising is examined through trust and confidence as well as sales. His conversation with David Serlin describes chance and control as intertwined practices rather than mutually exclusive eras, linking gambling, belief and economic life without claiming that calculation eliminates uncertainty.

named_group_routes.relationship: Antimodernism and the invented folk in twentieth-century Nova Scotia (1992, 1994)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: In-period evidence (1992, 1994). In 'Tartanism Triumphant' (Acadiensis, 1992; pp. 5–9 read) McKay asks how Nova Scotia 'became Scottish' in the second quarter of the twentieth century, when 'a collection of hazy generalizations and ethnic stereotypes' became 'a natural and obvious "commonsense"'. His broad answer: 'it was part of an international anti-modernist wave, a local version of a general middle-class search for something outside and better than the crisis-ridden modern world it inhabited' (pp. 8–9); the narrow answer is the state's cultural power under Angus L. Macdonald. Note 12 takes Lears's definition of American antimodernism and adds the 'simple life' and 'nature'. The Quest of the Folk (1994) is checked at summary and contents level: chapters on 'The Idea of the Folk', Helen Creighton and folklore, Mary Black and handicrafts, the simple life, and the folk 'under conditions of postmodernity'. Muise's review essay (Acadiensis, 1998; pp. 128–32 read) describes the three case studies and quotes the book's conclusion that 'the concept of the Folk was and remains a powerful obstacle to the formation of a counter-hegemonic cultural politics' (p. 306). Wright's 1995 Acadiensis review essay on English-Canadian intellectual history cites the book for 'a very skilled handling of Antonio Gramsci's theory of cultural hegemony by an historian' (p. 132 n. 29). A contribution to the field's cultural strand, not its origin: Berger, McKillop and Owram precede it. In the sampled corpus, 56 of 1,303 strict History doctoral dissertations dated 2009–2026 cite the book. Bibliographies record consultation, not influence. In the Province of History (2010, with Bates) is a later reading.

sources.title: Ian McKay, “Tartanism Triumphant: The Construction of Scottishness in Nova Scotia, 1933–1954,” Acadiensis 21, no. 2 (Spring 1992): 5–47.
sources.citation: Ian McKay, “Tartanism Triumphant: The Construction of Scottishness in Nova Scotia, 1933–1954,” Acadiensis 21, no. 2 (Spring 1992): 5–47.

verification.note: PDF citation line on p. 5: Acadiensis XXI, 2 (Spring 1992), pp. 5–47; author line Ian McKay. Pages 5–9 read closely, with notes 1–13. Nova Scotia 'became Scottish' in the second quarter of the twentieth century; 'hazy generalizations and ethnic stereotypes' became 'a natural and obvious "commonsense"'. Broad answer: 'it was part of an international anti-modernist wave, a local version of a general middle-class search for something outside and better than the crisis-ridden modern world it inhabited' (pp. 8–9). Narrow answer: Premier Angus L. Macdonald 'used the state's cultural power' to fuse a romantic, essentialist Scottishness with tourism (p. 9). Note 12 (p. 9) quotes Lears's definition of American antimodernism (No Place of Grace, p. xv) and adds 'and, I would also add, in the "simple life" and in "nature"'. Pages 13–14 and note 32 also read: the concept of 'invented tradition' is useful 'provided it is acknowledged that all traditions are historically constructed', and Trevor-Roper is said to rely on 'a naive historical realism'. Note 1: a revised version of a paper given to the CHA in 1990. The rest of the article was searched by keyword only, not read. Checked against: UNB Libraries Acadiensis article page and PDF (article/view/11913; PDF download 11913/12757).

sources.scope_note: McKay's own in-period statement of antimodernism as the frame for Nova Scotia's invented identity; his checked use of Lears.

sources.title: D. A. Muise, “Who Owns History Anyway? Reinventing Atlantic Canada for Pleasure and Profit,” Acadiensis 27, no. 2 (Spring 1998): 124–34.
sources.citation: D. A. Muise, “Who Owns History Anyway? Reinventing Atlantic Canada for Pleasure and Profit,” Acadiensis 27, no. 2 (Spring 1998): 124–34.

verification.note: Review essay; PDF citation line on p. 124 and signature 'D. A. MUISE'. Pages 124 and 128–32 read (the section on The Quest of the Folk). Muise writes that the book 'examines the origins of the essentialist folk tradition' and that McKay 'explodes the central place of the "folk" in understanding Nova Scotia's culture and history'. He describes three case studies (Helen Creighton, Mary Black and handicrafts, and literary producers including the Song Fishermen) and an afterword, 'The Folk under Conditions of Postmodernity'. McKay acknowledges a debt to Whisnant and Raymond Williams and places himself 'within a neo-marxist framework associated with the work of Antonio Gramsci'. Muise quotes the book (p. 306): 'the concept of the Folk was and remains a powerful obstacle to the formation of a counter-hegemonic cultural politics, without which a new, profoundly emancipatory politics of class, gender and racial equality is inconceivable.' Note 9 lists McKay's earlier essays on the theme (1988, 1992, 1993). Pages 125–27 not read; pp. 133–34 only glanced at (to the signature). Checked against: UNB Libraries Acadiensis article page and PDF (article/view/10846; PDF 10846/11670).

sources.scope_note: In-period reception of The Quest of the Folk; its closing argument quoted at p. 306.

sources.title: Donald Wright, “Discourse, Power and Tradition: Approach and Method in Recent English-Canadian Intellectual History,” Acadiensis 24, no. 2 (Spring 1995): 122–34.
sources.citation: Donald Wright, “Discourse, Power and Tradition: Approach and Method in Recent English-Canadian Intellectual History,” Acadiensis 24, no. 2 (Spring 1995): 122–34.

verification.note: Review essay on six other books (Valverde, Anderson, Vipond, Ferguson, Christian, Horton); The Quest of the Folk is not among them. Page 122 (opening, three approaches: discourse analysis, history of political thought, biography) and p. 132 read. Note 29 (p. 132): 'For a very skilled handling of Antonio Gramsci's theory of cultural hegemony by an historian see Ian McKay, The Quest of the Folk ... (Montreal and Kingston, 1994).' This is a footnote recommendation, not a review of the book. Checked against: UNB Libraries Acadiensis article page and PDF (article/view/12013; PDF 12013/12857). Addendum 2026-10-14: Valverde section re-read for the 1.135 person entry, pp. 122–126 (UNB PDF 12013/12857). Wright reviews The Age of Light, Soap, and Water as one of six books. Passages used: 'In her much talked about treatise'; the six authors include 'one a sociologist (Mariana Valverde)'; 'Following Foucault' (p. 122); 'Valverde is quick to avoid a "descent into discourse"'; she 'modifies Foucault's archaeology' and 'maintains an important commitment to social agency'; quotes the book's p. 43 on 'the decentring of the subject' (p. 123); quotes p. 166, '[m]oral regulation is an important aspect of ruling, helping to constitute class, gender, sexual, and race relations'; 'the concept of slippages', 'her most exciting, most original, contribution' (p. 124); her conclusion that audiences 'knew precisely what was meant' is 'untenable'; 'the impoverished immigrant and the "fallen woman" remain conspicuously silent' (p. 125); 'the silence of the consumer amidst the din of the producer gives the impression of top-down social control, precisely what Valverde sought to avoid' (p. 126).

sources.scope_note: In-period placement of The Quest of the Folk within English-Canadian intellectual history (a single note).
